html:
A significant escalation in the US-Iran conflict marks a critical juncture for global stability, with daily military strikes now entering their ninth consecutive day, resulting in US casualties and direct Iranian attacks on multiple Gulf states. This heightened tension is profoundly impacting international oil markets and threatening vital shipping lanes.

US-Iran Conflict: The United States has launched new strikes on Iran, including targeting an Iranian city home to a nuclear plant, prompting Iran to warn the US over the attack on its Darkhovin nuclear power project. Concurrently, Iran has conducted retaliatory attacks across the Gulf, striking Kuwait, Bahrain, and Jordan. These Iranian actions have reportedly caused injuries and damage to power and water plants in Kuwait, while Bahrain reported intercepting Iranian missiles and drones. Tragically, two US service members were killed and one is missing following Iranian strikes on Jordan, leading Trump to acknowledge the casualties and attribute them to fighting to prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon. Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicated that the US remains open to diplomacy despite the intensified military actions.

Strait of Hormuz: The Strait of Hormuz has become a focal point of the crisis, with two oil tankers reportedly exploding and another vessel catching fire. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards announced they have halted vessels and warned that no equipment or vessels intended for use against Iran will be permitted to transit the Strait. Rubio noted Iran is using the Strait as leverage, contributing to a sharp decrease in tanker traffic. This volatility has driven Brent crude prices up to $90.50 a barrel, briefly surpassing $91, reflecting global economic concerns over oil supply.

Russia-Ukraine: The conflict in the Black Sea has intensified, with Russian attacks on merchant ships killing ten people, and local authorities reporting 28 deaths in the Odesa region in July. Ukraine responded by targeting Moscow with 400 drones after a major attack on Kyiv, while Russia continued to pound Kyiv with ballistic missiles. This renewed violence on the Black Sea route raises concerns about global grain supply, as Ukraine has lost a third of its capacity to export grain via its Black Sea ports. Domestically, Zelenskyy's position is challenged as an ex-defense minister rejected an offer to return, and he faces pressure to remove his top general.

UK Politics & Great Powers: In a notable political transition, Andy Burnham has become the new United Kingdom prime minister, succeeding Keir Starmer. Burnham has pledged to end rough sleeping and characterized his arrival as a "circuit breaker" moment for the UK. Trump has conversed with Burnham, who invited him to visit. Separately, North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui met with Putin in a diplomatic push, leading to speculation about a possible visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to Russia.

Hamas Leadership: Amidst the wider Middle East tensions, Hamas has named Khalil al-Hayya as its new overall leader. Al-Hayya, identified as the group’s chief negotiator in Gaza talks and Iran-aligned, replaces Yahya Sinwar, who was killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in 2024.

Global Challenges: Thousands of mostly young people have marched on India's parliament in Delhi, demanding changes to the education system, with some protesters reporting injuries in clashes with police. Meanwhile, the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo continues to worsen, with at least 930 deaths reported out of 2,344 cases, prompting neighboring countries to boost preparedness measures.
